implementation_notes: Channels are the language's built-in event queue: make(chan Event, n) is a bounded FIFO whose send proceeds whenever the buffer is not full, a consumer ranges over it, closing the channel is the end-of-stream signal, and select with a default makes polling non-blocking. What replaces the classic structure is the channel itself - no queue class, no head/tail bookkeeping, and the synchronization is part of the language. An explicit slice queue is still justified when the drain must run in lock-step with a tick or the pending window must be coalesced.
pitfalls: A full buffered channel blocks the sender: fire-and-forget silently becomes back-pressure on unrelated systems - size the buffer and pick the drop policy deliberately.
Only the sender should close the channel, and only when no further sends can happen: closing twice or sending after close panics.
Draining in a goroutine makes handlers concurrent with senders, so any state they touch needs its own synchronization instead of the queue's happens-before edge.

variants.name: Slice backed FIFO drained per tick (single goroutine)
variants.idiom_name: []Event + head index, drained at a fixed point
variants.implementation_notes: When enqueue and drain happen on the same goroutine - the usual game-loop or per-tick simulation shape - a slice with a head index is the idiomatic queue: Post is an append, Drain walks the pending suffix and resets it, nothing blocks and the contents stay inspectable and replayable. It differs from the channel variant by giving up concurrency on purpose: determinism, no goroutine hand-off and no buffer-full failure mode, at the price of being confined to one goroutine.
pitfalls: q.items = q.items[:0] keeps the backing array and every payload it ever held reachable; nil the slice out or reuse it consciously when events reference large graphs.
Appending during Drain extends the loop you are iterating - handlers must post to a different queue or the drain must snapshot its bounds.
